results.title: Determining sample size for pilot trials: a tutorial | The BMJ
results.content: Because the goal of pilot trials is not to estimate or test intervention efficacy or effectiveness, traditional sample size calculations for definitive trials are not directly applicable.18 In practice, researchers frequently rely on rules of thumb, which might be suitable for some but not all pilot trials.1920 Sample size explanations are frequently absent in pilot trial reports.21. To ensure 95% confidence in observing at least one disagreement, the researchers calculate a sample size of 30 participants (15 per group for a two-group study, rounded up from 29 for 1:1 equal allocation) for the pilot trial (appendix 1 table 5). By definition, pilot trials have small sample sizes that result in imprecise estimates of effects, and pilot trials with promising results might be more likely to be published and cited in plans for definitive trials, so relying solely on effect point estimates from pilot trials can lead to suboptimal sample sizes for definitive trials.51525354 Rather, researchers should use clinically important differences between groups—informed by previous research and expert opinion—to determine effect sizes that should be used to calculate required sample sizes. To estimate variability for normally distributed outcomes, researchers can conduct a pilot trial with 12 or 35 participants per group to achieve reasonable precision and efficiency (appendix 2 box 1 includes more details).1137 Conservatively, the definitive trial’s sample size should be increased to mitigate the probability of being underpowered because the variability estimate comes from a small trial.38 When there is uncertainty in the variance estimate, blinded sample size re-estimation might be done after the definitive trial has started55; this approach uses the variance data collected during the trial to adjust the sample size as needed.56. In these studies, researchers establish targets for meaningful improvement and calculate the proportion of participants who meet those targets.14 In some contexts, researchers might conduct pilot trials of appropriate size to inform decisions about progression.42 This approach relies on the sample size calculation method proposed by Cocks and Torgerson42 that accounts for additional uncertainty in the effect size estimate. results.title: Gladia - Fine-Tuning ASR Models: Key Definitions, Mechanics, and Use Cases
results.content: The fine-tuning process involves taking an existing model and training it further on domain-specific data. During the fine-tuning process, a pre-trained ASR model with pre-trained weights is used. Since fine-tuning is done on a comparatively small (and domain-specific) dataset, the training is completed quicker than it takes to re-train the entire model. In such a case, we can add new layers) to the end of the model and just train them during the fine-tuning process. A fine-tuned model uses the language patterns learned from its earlier dataset and applies them to the new domain. It will load and process the data as required, update model weights, save the fine-tuned checkpoints and log the WER as per the provided arguments. Fine-tuning ASR models helps train them for downstream tasks with little use of resources and data. Fine-tuning allows the model to expand its knowledge base using new data and be used in a new domain or task.
